p.src: When Jia Rong saw that everything at home had been properly arranged, he hurried to the temple and reported to Jia Zhen. That very night, they assigned the various duties and attendants and prepared all the banners, carrying poles, and other necessary articles. They chose the hour of the Hare on the fourth day to escort the coffin into the city, while sending word to all their relatives and friends. On that day the funeral procession was dazzlingly magnificent and the guests gathered like clouds; from Iron Threshold Temple to the Ning mansion, tens of thousands lined the road to watch. Some among them sighed, others looked on with envy, while certain half-educated scholars declared that “in funeral rites, sorrowful simplicity is better than lavish display”; conflicting comments flew all along the road. They did not arrive until between the hours of the Goat and the Monkey, when the coffin was placed in the main hall. Once the offerings and formal lamentations were over, the relatives and friends gradually departed, leaving only members of the clan to attend to receiving and seeing off guests and other such duties. Of the close relatives, only Uncle Xing remained to keep them company. Bound now by the demands of ritual, Jia Zhen and Jia Rong had no choice but to lie beside the coffin on straw mats with clods of earth for pillows and endure the hardships of mourning. Yet after everyone had gone, they still seized every opportunity to fool around with the younger sisters of the deceased. Baoyu too wore mourning each day at the Ning mansion and returned to the Garden only in the evening, after the guests had dispersed. Xifeng had not yet recovered and could not attend constantly; but whenever there was a service with sutra chanting or a day on which relatives and friends came to present offerings, she forced herself to come and help Madam You manage affairs.

p.src: One day, after the morning meal had been offered, Jia Zhen and the others, exhausted by many days of toil and with the long summer day still ahead, inevitably dozed beside the coffin. Seeing that no guests were arriving, Baoyu decided to return home and see how Daiyu was, first stopping at Happy Red Court. When he entered, he found the courtyard silent and deserted. Several old women and young maids were taking advantage of the shade beneath the covered walk; some lay asleep, while others sat nodding off. Baoyu did not disturb them. Only Si'er noticed him and hurried forward to raise the curtain. Just as she was lifting it, Fangguan came running out from within, laughing, and almost collided headlong with Baoyu. Only when she saw Baoyu did she stop, still smiling, and say, “What brings you here? Quick, stop Qingwen for me! She wants to hit me.” Before she had finished speaking, a noisy clatter and crash came from inside, as though something had scattered all over the floor. Qingwen came racing after her, scolding, “Let me see where you little hussy can run! You lost and yet refuse your forfeit. With Baoyu away, let us see who will save you!” Baoyu hurriedly intercepted her with a smile. “Your little sister is young and may not know how she offended you. Spare her for my sake.” Qingwen had not expected Baoyu to return just then, and the sudden sight of him made her laugh. “Fangguan must be a vixen spirit in disguise! Not even a spell for summoning gods and dispatching generals could work so quickly.” Then she added with a laugh, “Even if you really have summoned a god, I am not afraid.” She broke free and tried once more to catch Fangguan. But Fangguan had already hidden behind Baoyu. Baoyu therefore took Qingwen by one hand and Fangguan by the other. Together they went inside. There, on the kang by the west wall, Sheyue, Qiuwen, Bihen, Zixiao, and the others were playing knucklebones, wagering melon seeds. It turned out that Fangguan had lost to Qingwen but had refused to submit to a slap and had run outside. In chasing Fangguan, Qingwen had spilled all the counters from the fold of her gown over the floor. Baoyu said delightedly, “The days are so long, and while I am away I worry that you will grow bored and make yourselves ill by sleeping after every meal. It is much better for everyone to find a game and amuse yourselves together.” Not seeing Xiren, he then asked, “Where is your sister Xiren?” “Xiren?” said Qingwen. “She has grown more solemn and virtuous than ever and is sitting alone in the room, contemplating the wall. I have not been in there for quite a while, so I do not know what she is doing. I cannot hear the least sound from her. Go and look quickly; perhaps she has attained enlightenment by now—who can say?” Laughing as he listened, Baoyu walked into the inner room. He found Xiren seated on the bed beside the window, holding a grey cord in her hands and tying ornamental knots.

p.src: When she saw Baoyu enter, she hurriedly rose and said with a smile, “What nonsense has that creature Qingwen been saying about me? I wanted to hurry and finish this knot and had no time to join in their foolish games, so I teased them by saying, ‘You go and play. While Second Master is away, I shall sit quietly here for a while and rest my spirits.’ Then she invented all that rubbish about my ‘contemplating the wall’ and ‘practising Chan meditation.’ Just wait—I shall tear that mouth of hers!” Baoyu smilingly sat down close beside Xiren and watched her work on the knot. “On such a long day, you ought to rest awhile, or laugh and play with the others. Otherwise, it would be good to visit Cousin Lin. It is terribly hot—what need is there to work on that now?” “I noticed,” Xiren replied, “that the fan case you carry is still the one made in the year of young Mistress Rong's funeral at the eastern mansion. That blue one is suitable only when a member of the clan or a relative or friend has a death in the family during summer. You may wear it once or twice a year on such occasions, but there is no need to make one ordinarily. But now that there is a funeral at that mansion, you must go there wearing it every day, so I am hurrying to make another. Once I have finished the knot, I shall replace that old one for you. You may pay no attention to such matters, but if the Old Lady sees it when she returns, she will say once again that we are lazy and take no care even over what you wear and carry.” Baoyu smiled. “It was truly thoughtful of you to remember. But you must not rush too much. Overheating yourself would be far more serious.” As he spoke, Fangguan arrived carrying a cup of tea freshly chilled in cold water. Baoyu had always been delicate by constitution, so even in the hottest months he did not dare use ice. Instead, the teapot was immersed in a basin of freshly drawn well water, which was changed from time to time merely to lend the tea some coolness. Baoyu drank half a cup from Fangguan's hand, then said to Xiren, “Before I came, I instructed Mingyan to send word at once if any important guest should arrive at Cousin Zhen's. If nothing important happens, I shall not go back there.” Having said this, he went out of the room, then turned back and called to Bihen and the others, “If anything happens, come and find me at Miss Lin's.” He then went straight to the Naiad's House to visit Daiyu.

p.src: As he was about to cross Qinfang Bridge, he saw Xueyan leading two old serving-women, each carrying water chestnuts, lotus roots, melons, fruit, and the like. Baoyu hurriedly asked Xueyan, “Your young lady never eats such cooling foods. What are these melons and fruits for? Surely she is not entertaining some young lady or married mistress?” Xueyan smiled. “I will tell you, but you must not let on to my young lady.” Baoyu nodded his promise. Xueyan then told the two women, “Take the melons and fruit ahead and give them to Sister Zijuan. If she asks where I am, say that I am attending to something and will be there presently.” The women assented and went off. Only then did Xueyan say, “Our young lady has just begun to feel a little better these past two days. After the meal today, Third Miss came and invited her to visit Second Mistress, but she did not go. Then something unknown came to mind and made her melancholy for a while; she took up her brush and wrote a great deal, though I do not know whether it was poetry or some other kind of verse. When she sent me for the melons and fruit, I also heard her tell Zijuan to remove the ornaments from the little qin table in her room, move the table into the middle of the outer room, and set the dragon-patterned tripod censer upon it, ready for when the fruit arrived. If she means to entertain someone, there is no reason to hurry and set out a censer beforehand. If she means to burn incense, our young lady ordinarily displays only fresh flowers, fruit, quinces, and such things in her room, and she is not fond of perfuming her clothes; even if she did burn incense, it ought to be where she usually sits or sleeps. Surely the old women have not made the room stink so badly that she needs incense to fumigate it! In truth, even I do not know the reason.” Having said this, she hurried away. Baoyu lowered his head and pondered, “Judging by what Xueyan said, there must be some reason for it. If she were merely sitting with one of the other girls, there would be no need to prepare the offerings and vessels beforehand. Perhaps it is the death anniversary of her father or mother; yet I remember that every year when those dates come round, the Old Lady orders special dishes prepared and sent to Cousin Lin for her private rites, and those dates have already passed. Most likely, since it is the seventh month, the season of melons and fruit, when every family makes autumn offerings at its ancestral graves, Cousin Lin has been moved to perform a private offering in her own room, perhaps in the spirit of the Book of Rites: ‘In spring and autumn they offer the foods of the season.’ But if I go to her now and find her grieving, I shall do my utmost to console her, yet I fear her vexation may become pent up in her heart; if I do not go, I fear she may grieve too deeply with no one to restrain or comfort her. Either course might make her ill. I had better first visit Sister Feng, sit there for a short while, and then return. If I then find Cousin Lin grieving, I shall think of some way to comfort her, so that she may give some vent to her sorrow without grieving excessively, and may not fall ill from suppressing it.” His mind made up, he left the garden gate and went straight to Sister Feng’s quarters.

p.src: A number of senior serving-women had just finished reporting household business and were streaming out. Xifeng was leaning against the doorway, talking with Pinger. As soon as she saw Baoyu, she smiled and said, “So you have come back. I had just given instructions to Lin Zhixiao’s wife. I told her to send word to the page attending you that, if you had nothing to do, he should take the opportunity to ask you to come back and rest awhile. Besides, there are so many people there; how could you endure all those smells? And now, unexpectedly, here you are.” Baoyu smiled. “Thank you, Sister, for thinking of me. I had nothing to do today, and when I noticed that you had not gone over to the other residence these past two days, I wondered whether you had fully recovered, so I came back to see how you were.” Xifeng said, “I am much the same as ever—well for three days and unwell for two. With the Old Lady and Her Ladyship away, these women—ah, which one of them behaves herself? Every day, if they are not fighting, they are quarreling; there have even been two or three uproars over gambling and theft. Third Miss may be helping to manage affairs, but she is still an unmarried young lady. Some matters may properly be brought to her attention, while others cannot be spoken of to her, so I can only struggle on as best I can. I never get a moment’s peace. Never mind hoping to recover; I shall be satisfied if I merely grow no worse.” Baoyu said, “Even so, Sister, you must take care of yourself and worry less over these affairs.” After saying this, he chatted for a while longer, took leave of Xifeng, and headed straight back into the garden.

p.src: When he entered the courtyard of the Xiaoxiang Lodge, he saw the last wisps of smoke curling from the censer and fine wine left over from the libation. Zijuan was supervising the servants as they carried the table back inside and put away the ritual furnishings. Baoyu knew at once that the rite was over. Entering the room, he saw Daiyu reclining with her face turned inward, languid with illness and looking utterly overcome. Zijuan hastily announced, “Master Bao is here.” Only then did Daiyu slowly sit up and invite him to be seated with a smile. Baoyu asked, “Have you been much better these last two days, Cousin? Your complexion does look calmer, but why have you been grieving again?” Daiyu replied, “You must have run out of things to say. When have I been grieving, when everything is perfectly well?” Baoyu smiled. “There are tear stains plainly visible on your face, Cousin. How can you still try to deceive me? I only think that, since you have always been delicate, you ought to take a more open view of everything and not indulge too deeply in fruitless sorrow. If you ruin your health and make me…” At this point, he felt that what followed would be difficult to say and hastily swallowed the words. For although he and Daiyu had grown up together, were perfectly attuned in feeling, and wished to share even life and death, all this had only been understood in their hearts and had never been spoken face to face. Moreover, Daiyu was sensitive and suspicious, and his impulsive remarks had often offended her. He had come today expressly to comfort her, yet had unexpectedly spoken rashly again and could not finish his sentence; in his agitation, he also feared that Daiyu would be angry with him. Then, reflecting that his intentions had truly been kind, his agitation turned to sorrow, and tears were already rolling down his cheeks. At first Daiyu had been annoyed that Baoyu spoke without weighing the seriousness of his words; but when she saw him in this state, she was deeply moved. Being naturally prone to tears, she too could not help weeping silently with him.

p.src: Just then Zijuan came in carrying tea. Supposing that the two of them had quarreled over something again, she said, “Miss, you have only just begun to feel better, and now Master Bao has come to upset you again. What in the world is going on?” Wiping away his tears, Baoyu replied with a smile, “Who would dare upset my dear cousin?” At the same time, he rose with an awkward attempt to change the subject and began strolling about. Noticing the corner of a sheet of paper protruding slightly from beneath the inkstone, he could not resist reaching out and picking it up. Daiyu hurriedly rose to snatch it back, but Baoyu had already tucked it inside his robe. He pleaded with a smile, “Dear cousin, please let me have a look.” Daiyu said, “Whatever it is, the moment you arrive you rummage through everything.” Before she had finished speaking, Baochai appeared and asked with a smile, “What is Cousin Bao so eager to see?” Baoyu had not yet seen what was written on the paper and did not know how Daiyu felt about it, so he dared not answer rashly and merely looked at her with a smile. As Daiyu invited Baochai to sit down, she explained with a smile, “In the old histories I have read of many talented and beautiful women whose lifelong fortunes inspire delight and admiration, sorrow and lamentation. Having nothing to do after the meal today, I thought I would select a few of them and cobble together some verses to express my feelings. Just then that girl Tanchun came to ask me to visit Sister Feng with her, but I felt listless and did not go. I had just finished five poems when I grew drowsy and left them lying there. I never imagined Second Master would arrive and see them. There is really no harm in letting him read them; I only dislike his copying things out indiscriminately and showing them to other people.” Baoyu hastily protested, “When have I ever shown them to anyone? As for that fan yesterday, I loved those poems on the white begonias, so I copied them onto it myself in small regular script, simply because it would be convenient to hold and read. Surely I know that poems and handwriting from the women’s apartments must not lightly be circulated outside. Ever since you spoke to me about it, I have never taken the fan out of the Garden.” Baochai said, “Cousin Lin is right to be concerned about that. Once you have written them on a fan, you might absentmindedly carry it into the study, and if the gentlemen there saw it, how could they fail to ask who composed the poems? If word of them were to spread, it would be unseemly. As the old saying goes, ‘A woman’s virtue lies in having no talent.’ Chastity and composure come first, and needlework is only the second consideration. Poetry and the like are merely diversions of the inner chambers; one may know how to compose them or not. Girls from families such as ours have no need of a reputation for literary talent.” Then, turning to Daiyu with a smile, she added, “There is no harm in bringing them out for me to see, so long as Cousin Bao is not allowed to take them away.” Daiyu laughed. “If that is what you say, then you need not see them either.” Then, pointing at Baoyu, she added with a smile, “He has already snatched them away.” Only then did Baoyu take the paper from inside his robe. Moving close beside Baochai, he read it carefully together with her.

Li Wan, Xifeng, Baochai, Daiyu, Yingchun, Tanchun, Xichun, and the others were already waiting in the central hall, and he exchanged greetings with each of them. The third sister responded only with indifference, but the second was very much inclined toward him. There were too many eyes upon them, however, and no opportunity to act. p.src: One day, a junior steward named Yu Lu came to report to Jia Zhen: “The awning poles, mourning cloth, bearers, and their blue garments used earlier cost a total of one thousand one hundred and ten taels of silver. You might order the money advanced from your private treasury for the present, or tell me which account I may borrow it from, so that I will know how to proceed.” Jia Zhen laughed. “You still think this is the old days, when silver lay idle waiting to be spent. p.src: Jia Lian entered the Ning mansion, where the chief steward had already assembled the servants to greet him; they clustered around him all the way to the main hall. Jia Lian asked each of them a few perfunctory questions, merely for form's sake, then dismissed the servants and went farther inside alone. Jia Lian and Jia Zhen had always been close, and as they were kinsmen with no need for reserve between them, Jia Lian never waited to be announced. When he reached the principal apartments, an old maidservant waiting in the corridor promptly raised the curtain and admitted him. Entering the room, Jia Lian saw Second Sister You sitting on the kang to the south, sewing with two maids; neither old Madam You nor Third Sister was there. Jia Lian hurried forward to exchange greetings with her. Second Sister You smilingly invited him to sit, then seated herself beside the screen on the eastern side. Jia Lian insisted that Second Sister take the place of honor. After a few polite remarks, he asked with a smile, “Where have your mother and Third Sister gone? Why do I not see them?” Second Sister You replied with a smile, “They had some business in the back just now. They will be here presently.” The attending maids had gone to pour tea, leaving no one nearby, and Jia Lian kept casting sidelong glances at Second Sister. Second Sister lowered her head and merely smiled, paying him no heed. Jia Lian did not dare presume to touch her. Seeing her toy with a silk handkerchief to which a purse was tied, he made conversation by feeling at his waist and saying, “I forgot to bring my betel-nut purse. If you have any betel, little sister, be kind enough to give me a piece.” Second Sister said, “I do have betel nuts, but I never give mine to anyone.”

p.src: Now Jia Rong, seeing that Yu Lu had gone with Jia Lian to fetch the silver and having nothing himself to do, returned inside, where he joked and flirted for a while with his two aunts before taking his leave. That evening he returned to the temple and reported to Jia Zhen, “The silver has already been handed over to Yu Lu. The old lady has nearly recovered and is no longer taking medicine.” Having said this, he took the opportunity to mention Jia Lian’s proposal, made on the road, to take Second Sister You as a secondary wife. He explained that Jia Lian would buy a house for her outside the family compound and keep it secret from Xifeng, adding, “For the present, this is all being considered because it has been so difficult for him to obtain an heir. Besides, we already know Second Aunt, and a marriage between relatives is better than accepting a proposal from some unknown family elsewhere. That is why Second Uncle repeatedly begged me to speak to Father about it.” He did not say that the idea had actually been his own. Jia Zhen considered the matter and said with a smile, “There is really no harm in it. The only question is whether your second aunt herself is willing. Tomorrow, first discuss it with your grandmother; have her ascertain your second aunt’s wishes, and then we shall decide.” He then coached Jia Rong in what he should say and went over to tell Lady You about the matter. Lady You knew that the arrangement was improper and did all she could to dissuade him. But Jia Zhen had already made up his mind, and she was accustomed to yielding to him. Moreover, Second Sister was not born of the same mother as she, so she was in no position to interfere too deeply; consequently, she could only let them carry on as they pleased. Early the next morning, Jia Rong duly returned to the city to see his grandmother and conveyed his father’s proposal to her. He embellished it with a great many claims: how admirable a man Jia Lian was; how Xifeng was now ill and could never recover; and how, for the time being, they would buy a house outside for Second Aunt to live in, but after a year or eighteen months, as soon as Xifeng died, she would be brought into the mansion as his principal wife. He also described how his father would arrange the betrothal, how Jia Lian would conduct the wedding, how they would take the old lady in and support her in her old age, and how in due course they would also undertake to find a husband for Third Sister. His glowing account was so extravagant that old Mrs. You could hardly refuse. Besides, she had always depended entirely on Jia Zhen’s support; now Jia Zhen himself was arranging the match, she would not have to provide a dowry, and Jia Lian was a young gentleman ten times superior to Zhang Hua. She therefore hurried over to consult Second Sister. Second Sister was fickle by nature and had already had an improper relationship with her brother-in-law. She had also often regretted having been mistakenly promised to Zhang Hua, which had left her with no settled future. Now that she saw Jia Lian was enamoured of her, and that her brother-in-law himself was arranging her marriage, why should she object? She nodded her consent. They immediately sent their answer to Jia Rong, and Jia Rong reported it to his father.

p.src: The next day, Jia Lian was invited to the temple, where Jia Zhen personally told him that old Mrs. You had given her consent. Jia Lian was naturally beside himself with joy and thanked Jia Zhen and Jia Rong, father and son, profusely. The two of them then made arrangements to have a house inspected and jewellery fashioned, and to purchase a dowry for Second Sister as well as a bed, curtains, and the other furnishings required for the bridal chamber. In no more than a few days, all the preparations had been completed. A house of more than twenty rooms had been purchased in Little Flower-Branch Lane, about two li behind Ning-Rong Street. Two young maidservants were also purchased. Then Jia Lian suddenly remembered his servant Bao Er. Bao Er’s former wife had once committed adultery with Jia Lian; after Xifeng created a violent scene over the affair, the woman hanged herself for shame. Jia Lian had instructed Lin Zhixiao to promise two hundred taels toward her funeral expenses, had privately given Bao Er some additional silver, and had promised to choose another wife for him later. Bao Er had thus preserved his standing and received money as well, so he continued to curry favour with Jia Lian. Remembering him now, Jia Lian summoned Bao Er and his wife to the new house so that they would be ready to attend upon Second Sister when she arrived. They also sent for Zhang Hua and his father and coerced them into writing old Mrs. You a formal renunciation of the engagement. Now Zhang Hua’s grandfather had originally served as the headman of an imperial grain estate, but had since died. When Zhang Hua’s father succeeded to the same post, he was on friendly terms with old Mrs. You’s former husband; consequently, Zhang Hua and Second Sister You were betrothed before either was born. Later, however, the family unexpectedly became embroiled in a lawsuit and lost its property, until it could scarcely afford food and clothing; how could they possibly bear the expense of bringing home a bride? Old Mrs. You had also remarried out of that household, and the two families had had no word of each other for more than ten years. Now that the Jia household’s servants had summoned them and forced Zhang Hua to break his engagement to Second Sister, he was unwilling at heart; but, fearing the power and arrogance of Jia Zhen and the others, he dared not disobey and had no choice but to write out a formal agreement dissolving the betrothal. Old Mrs. You gave them twenty taels of silver, and with that the engagement between the two families was dissolved.
